title: A Simple Compiler for CCA2-Secure Pseudorandom Codes in the Standard Model
authors: Nico Döttling, Antoine Joux, Venkata Koppula, Mahesh Sreekumar Rajasree, and Hendrik Waldner
abstract:
Public-key pseudorandom codes (PRCs) combine two seemingly conflicting properties: their codewords are computationally indistinguishable from uniformly random strings, yet a secret-key decoder can recover the encoded message even after a bounded Hamming corruption. Security against chosen-plaintext (CPA) attacks asks that an encoding of a chosen message appears uniform. Security against adaptive chosen-ciphertext (CCA2) attacks additionally gives
the adversary adaptive access to a decoding oracle for codewords outside the Hamming ball around the challenge encoding. Döttling et al. (CRYPTO 2026) showed how to realize CCA2-secure PRCs in the standard model through a generic compiler based on the Koppula-Waters hinting pseudorandom generator framework.

We give a substantially simpler black-box compiler. Starting from any adaptively $\alpha$-robust, CPA-pseudorandom PRC and using only a secure PRG and an almost perfectly correct IND-CCA2-secure PKE scheme, our compiler constructs an adaptively $\alpha/2$-robust, $\alpha/2$-CCA2-pseudorandom PRC. The compiled PRC has twice the codeword length of the underlying PRC and therefore loses only a factor of two in its relative decoding radius; in particular, it preserves a constant relative decoding radius.

                                                  Abstract
        Public-key pseudorandom codes (PRCs) combine two seemingly conflicting properties: their
     codewords are computationally indistinguishable from uniformly random strings, yet a secret-key
     decoder can recover the encoded message even after a bounded Hamming corruption. Security
     against chosen-plaintext (CPA) attacks asks that an encoding of a chosen message appears
     uniform. Security against adaptive chosen-ciphertext (CCA2) attacks additionally gives the
     adversary adaptive access to a decoding oracle for codewords outside the Hamming ball around
     the challenge encoding. Döttling et al. (CRYPTO 2026) showed how to realize CCA2-secure
     PRCs in the standard model through a generic compiler based on the Koppula–Waters hinting
     pseudorandom generator framework.
        We give a substantially simpler black-box compiler. Starting from any adaptively α-robust,
     CPA-pseudorandom PRC and using only a secure PRG and an almost perfectly correct IND-
     CCA2-secure PKE scheme, our compiler constructs an adaptively α/2-robust, α/2-CCA2-
     pseudorandom PRC. The compiled PRC has twice the codeword length of the underlying PRC
     and therefore loses only a factor of two in its relative decoding radius; in particular, it preserves
     a constant relative decoding radius.


1    Introduction
Error correction and pseudorandomness impose seemingly conflicting requirements. An error-
correcting code must contain enough structure to recover from noise, whereas a pseudorandom
string should reveal no efficiently detectable structure. Pseudorandom codes (PRCs), introduced by
Christ and Gunn [CG24], realize these seemingly contradictory properties within a single primitive:
encodings appear uniform, while a secret-key decoder can recover the desired message from noisy
encodings. Besides their original motivation in robust watermarking, PRCs have emerged as a useful
cryptographic primitive in their own right [LSW26].

Chosen-ciphertext security. The basic public-key security experiment asks an adversary to
distinguish an encoding of a chosen message from a uniformly random codeword. Chosen-ciphertext
security additionally gives the adversary adaptive access to the decoder. As observed by Alrabiah

                                                      1
et al. [AAC+ 25a], the appropriate oracle restriction differs from that for ordinary CCA2-secure
encryption. In the standard CCA2 experiment, the decryption oracle remains available after the
challenge but rejects the challenge ciphertext itself. A PRC adversary, however, can change a few
symbols of the challenge and obtain a different codeword that must decode to the same message. The
post-challenge oracle must therefore reject an entire Hamming ball around the challenge. Outside
this ball, the oracle remains available, and its answers must not reveal whether the challenge is a
genuine codeword or a uniform string.
    Alrabiah et al. [AAC+ 25a] introduced stronger decoding-oracle notions, including CCA2 security
for public-key PRCs, and gave a construction in the random-oracle model using the Fujisaki–Okamoto
transformation [FO99]. Döttling et al. [DJK+ 26a] subsequently obtained CCA2-secure PRCs in the
standard model. Their generic compiler starts from an adaptively robust, CPA-secure PRC and
adapts the hinting-PRG framework of Koppula and Waters [KW19]. The resulting construction
uses a hinting PRG, equivocal commitments, a one-time signature scheme, pseudorandom functions,
public-key encryption, and error-correcting codes. The construction presented by the authors is
quite technically involved and also reduces the error-correction rate quite significantly, which leads
to the following question:

Can one realize CCA2-secure PRCs in the standard model through a simple black-box compiler from
                            a small set of conventional primitives?

1.1   Our Results
We answer this question affirmatively. Our compiler only requires a CPA-secure PRC scheme, a
CCA2-secure PKE scheme and a PRG. All those primitives are used in a black-box manner and
our resulting scheme loses only a factor of two in the relative decoding radius compared to the
underlying PRC scheme. Informally:

Theorem 1.1 (Informal). Let PRCcpa be a public-key PRC over a finite alphabet Σ of codeword
length n that is CPA-pseudorandom and adaptively α-robust. Given an almost perfectly correct IND-
CCA2-secure PKE and a secure PRG, there is a black-box construction in the standard model of a
public-key PRC over Σ of codeword length 2n that is adaptively α2 -robust and α2 -CCA2-pseudorandom.

    The three ingredients play complementary roles. The underlying PRC makes the transmitted
blocks pseudorandom and robust to Hamming corruption. The IND-CCA2-secure PKE is used to
achieve the CCA security of the overall construction; its ciphertexts do need not be pseudorandom
or error tolerant because they will be placed inside the PRC encryption. Finally, the PRG is used
to generate the underlying encoder’s randomness via a fixed-length seed. Without this compression,
the length of the PKE ciphertext and the amount of randomness needed to encode that ciphertext
would be defined circularly, resulting in a compiler that cannot directly be instantiated.
    Our compiler is based on the CCA-secure encryption construction of Hohenberger, Lewko, and
Waters [HLW12]. In a nutshell, our compiler generates two independent key pairs for the base
PRC and one key pair for the PKE. To encode a message, it samples two PRG seeds, encrypts the
message together with these seeds, and encodes the resulting PKE ciphertext once under each PRC
key using the PRG expansion of the corresponding seed as randomness. The decoder recovers the
inner ciphertext from one block, decrypts it, expands the two seeds, and re-encodes both blocks. It
accepts only if the complete re-encoding is close to the received codeword. We provide a detailed
technical overview in the next section.

Scope of the simplification. Compared with the compiler of Döttling et al. [DJK+ 26a], our
construction requires no hinting PRG, equivocal commitment, one-time signature, PRF, or auxiliary
error-correcting layer. Besides the underlying PRC, it uses only a conventional IND-CCA2-secure
PKE and a standard PRG. This is a structural and proof-level simplification, not a claim that
the overall assumptions are weaker or that every instantiation improves the concrete rate, key size,
or running time. Our contribution is primarily conceptual: the transformation is black-box, only
doubles the codeword length, and maps an underlying relative decoding radius α to α2 .

1.2    Related Work
In this section, we recap the works on the general realization of PRCs, as well as works constructing
CCA-secure schemes specifically.
    Christ and Gunn [CG24] introduced private- and public-key PRCs and gave constructions robust
to a constant rate of substitution errors. A line of subsequent work broadened both the constructions
and the error models. Ghentiyala and Guruswami [GG24] gave new PRC constructions, and
Golowich and Moitra [GM24] lifted PRCs robust to substitution errors into ones robust against edit
errors (insertions and deletions) via an indexing technique, motivated by watermarking language
models. Christ, Golowich, Gunn, Moitra, and Wichs [CGG+ 25] obtained improved pseudorandom
codes from permuted puzzles. More recently, Dyseryn, Francati, and Venturi [DFV26] gave public-
key PRCs from distorted McEliece assumptions, and Huang, Li, Mao, and Zhou [HLMZ26] gave
high-rate public-key PRCs for edit errors.
    On the negative side, Garg, Gunn, and Wang [GGW25] showed that black-box use of standard
cryptographic primitives is insufficient to build PRCs, and Döttling, Müller, and Rajasree [DMR25]
gave an oracle separation ruling out PRC constructions relative to local oracles.
    On the security side, Alrabiah et al. [AAC+ 25a] developed the ideal-PRC viewpoint and stronger
decoding-oracle notions, including public-key chosen-ciphertext security. Döttling et al. [DJK+ 26a]
obtained CCA2-secure PRCs in the standard model through a generic compiler based on the
Koppula–Waters framework [KW19] and separately introduced the noisy-McEliece assumption
family. Concurrently, Chen, Mao, and Yi [CMY26] obtained standard-model public-key PRCs with
pre-challenge CCA1 security rather than full CCA2 security. A comparison between the mentioned
works that achieve CCA security as well as the compiler presented in this work is given in Table 1.

2     Technical Overview
Our construction follows the high-level paradigm of Hohenberger, Lewko, and Waters [HLW12]. We
first recall their approach and then explain how its encrypted-randomness consistency mechanism
can be adapted to the PRC setting.

2.1   The Hohenberger–Lewko–Waters Paradigm
Hohenberger, Lewko, and Waters introduce detectable chosen-ciphertext (DCCA) security for public-
key encryption. A detectable PKE scheme augments the usual algorithms with a public detection
algorithm F . Given a public key, a challenge ciphertext ct∗ , and another ciphertext ct, the algorithm
identifies whether ct may be useful for attacking ct∗ . Informally, DCCA security has two components.
First, before seeing ct∗ , it should be hard to produce a ciphertext that F will later classify as related
to ct∗ . Second, the challenge plaintext should remain hidden when the decryption oracle rejects
every ciphertext that F classifies as related to ct∗ .
    Their generic compiler achieves full CCA2 security by combining three encryption schemes: an
inner DCCA-secure scheme, an outer scheme with one-bounded chosen-ciphertext (1B-CCA) security,
and an outer CPA secure scheme. Here, one-bounded security permits the adversary at most one
decryption query. Setup generates independent key pairs (pkDCCA , skDCCA ), (pk1B-CCA , sk1B-CCA ),
and (pkCPA , skCPA ) for the three schemes.

    As observed by Hohenberger, Lewko, and Waters, this construction combines the two-key

encrypted randomness takes the place of a public consistency proof: after recovering the inner
ciphertext, the receiver can privately verify that both outer ciphertexts were honestly generated
from the same value.

Security argument. DCCA security protects the inner challenge ciphertext provided that the
adversary cannot submit a useful ciphertext that the detection algorithm marks as related to it. The
outer layers must therefore prevent an accepted decryption query from exposing such a related inner
ciphertext. The one-bounded chosen-ciphertext-secure component and the embedded-randomness
check jointly rule out this event. Moreover, a consistent ciphertext can be recovered through either
outer secret key, allowing the proof to switch its decryption path.
    The embedded randomness also creates the central proof difficulty: the outer challenge ciphertexts
use randomness contained in the inner challenge ciphertext, so the layers cannot be changed
independently in a direct hybrid argument. Hohenberger, Lewko, and Waters address this dependency
through an intermediate experiment called nested indistinguishability. There, the inner ciphertext
encrypts either the message together with the outer randomness or an all-zero string of the same
length, while the outer ciphertexts are formed exactly as in the actual construction. This experiment
lets the proof analyze “dangerous” decryption queries after removing the embedded information
and then transfer the conclusion back to the real distribution.

2.2    Adapting the Paradigm to Pseudorandom Codes
Although our compiler shares its high-level structure with the Hohenberger–Lewko–Waters paradigm,
its symmetric outer layer is, in one respect, even closer to the Naor–Yung two-key paradigm. In
more detail, we rely on two independently keyed instances of the same PRC encode the same
inner ciphertext and provide two decoding paths. Moreover, the randomness encrypted in the
inner ciphertext can be viewed as a privately verifiable consistency proof. After recovering this
randomness, or, in our final construction, the corresponding PRG seeds, the decoder re-encodes
both outer blocks and accepts only if the reconstructed pair is sufficiently close to the received
codeword. The recovered values thus act as a hidden consistency witness.
    To realize this idea for PRCs, our compiler places a full IND-CCA2-secure PKE in the inner
layer and two independently keyed instances of an adaptively robust, CPA-pseudorandom PRC
over a finite alphabet Σ in the outer layer. The PKE protects the logical payload, while the PRCs
turn its ciphertext into a pseudorandom codeword that remains decodable after bounded Hamming
corruption.

Security intuition. As already noted, our compiler is structurally close to the Naor–Yung
paradigm [NY90]: its two outer components are independently keyed instances of the same PRC
and therefore provide symmetric, interchangeable decoding paths for the same inner ciphertext. The
security proof exploits precisely this two-path structure. It first filters the inner challenge ciphertext:
any query recovering that ciphertext and passing the global check must lie in the Hamming ball
already excluded by the CCA2 experiment. The IND-CCA2 security of the PKE can then replace
the inner payload by zeros. Next, while decoder queries are answered through the first block, CPA
pseudorandomness replaces the second challenge block by a uniform codeword. Adaptive robustness
then permits the proof to switch to the second decoding path, after which CPA pseudorandomness
replaces the first challenge block by a uniform codeword as well. Finally, the proof switches back
to the original decoding path and removes the filter. Adaptive robustness ensures that the two
decoding paths agree on every query accepted by the global consistency check, except with negligible
probability. Thus, the second block does not improve the decoding radius; it provides the alternate
path needed by this Naor–Yung-style hybrid argument.
    For correctness alone, adaptive robustness of the first keyed PRC instance would suffice because
the real decoder begins with the first block. The CCA2 proof, however, switches between the two
decoding paths and therefore needs adaptive robustness for both independently keyed instances.

2.3   A Caveat on Instantiability
For the “direct randomness-encrypting construction” we can formally prove security and correctness
as argued above. There is one small caveat that remains though.
    To instantiate the PKE, we must first fix its plaintext length ℓmsg + 2ℓEnc , which determines its
ciphertext length ℓct . To determine ℓEnc , however, we must first instantiate the underlying PRC for
messages of exactly ℓct bits. Thus, the PKE ciphertext length depends on the randomness length of
the PRC instance, while that randomness length may itself depend on the PKE ciphertext length.
This creates a circular dependency for which it is not clear how to resolve it using the mentioned
primitives directly. Therefore, our above described construction is not a generally instantiable
black-box compiler.
    We remove this circularity using a standard PRG G : {0, 1}λ → {0, 1}ℓEnc . Instead of encrypting
the full encoder randomness, the encoder samples independent seeds s0 , s1 ← {0, 1}λ and computes

                      ccca ← PKE.Enc(pkcca , (msg, s0 , s1 )),
                        cb := PRCcpa .Encode(pkb , ccca ; G(sb ))    for b ∈ {0, 1}.

The decoder now parses the inner plaintext as (msg, s0 , s1 ) and expands the recovered seeds when
reconstructing the two outer blocks.
    The PKE plaintext length is now the fixed quantity ℓmsg + 2λ, which first determines the PKE

    In addition to CCA security, we require our PKE scheme to satisfy a property that we call
unpredictability. Informally, unpredictability states that, for any efficiently computable plaintext
family x = x(λ), even given the public key and the plaintext, the probability of predicting the exact

an average generated key-pair.
    This type of requirement was originally introduced in the work of Fujisaki and Okamoto [FO13],
who defined spreadness. Their notion requires that, for every public key in the support of key
generation and every plaintext, the probability of any particular ciphertext occurring under fresh
encryption randomness is negligible. Consequently, spreadness implies our unpredictability notion.
It is, however, a stronger requirement, since it imposes a worst-case bound over both public keys
and plaintexts.

4.1   Concrete Instantiation
Theorem 4.2 is generic—it compiles any adaptively robust, CPA-pseudorandom PRC PRCcpa , any
secure PRG G, and any almost perfectly correct IND-CCA2-secure PKE PKE into an α2 -CCA2-
pseudorandom PRC. All three ingredients are available from standard assumptions.

  1. The underlying PRC PRCcpa which is an adaptively robust CPA-pseudorandom PRC, can be
     instantiated from:
      (a) the Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) assumption [AAC+ 25a],
      (b) the noisy-McEliece assumption [DJK+ 26a].
  2. The PRG G can be instantiated from any one-way function [HILL99] and, therefore, a variety
     of concrete assumptions.
  3. The inner PKE PKE, an almost perfectly correct IND-CCA2-secure scheme is available from a
     wide range of assumptions. Direct constructions, each with (almost) perfect correctness, are
     known from:
      (a) the Decisional Diffie–Hellman assumption, via the Cramer–Shoup cryptosystem [CS98]
          and, more generally, hash-proof systems [CS02],
      (b) the Quadratic Residuosity and Decisional Composite Residuosity assumptions, via the
          universal hash-proof framework [CS02],
       (c) the hardness of factoring, via the practical scheme of Hofheinz and Kiltz [HK09],
      (d) the Learning With Errors assumption [Reg05], via lossy and correlated-input trapdoor
          functions [PW08, MP12],
       (e) the (low-noise) Learning Parity with Noise assumption, via the schemes of Kiltz, Masny,
           and Pietrzak [KMP14] and of Yu and Zhang [YZ16];
       (f) the McEliece assumption, via the CCA2-secure variant of the McEliece cryptosystem of
           Döttling et al. [DDMN12].
      Some assumptions are not known to yield IND-CCA2 security on their own and instead reach
      it through a generic transformation applied to a weaker primitive:
      (a) any enhanced trapdoor permutation, or any CPA-secure PKE together with a NIZK
          proof system, via the double-encryption paradigm of Naor and Yung [NY90] and its
          adaptively secure realization by Dolev, Dwork, and Naor [DDN91];
      (b) the Computational Diffie–Hellman assumption, and generically any CPA-secure PKE,
          via the hinting-PRG compiler of Koppula and Waters [KW19];
       (c) any identity-based encryption scheme, via the Canetti–Halevi–Katz transform [CHK04].
